evals.prompt: I have the titanic data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet. Fit an XGBoost classifier predicting survival from pclass, sex, and age with a 70/30 stratified train/test split. Use conservative hyperparameters (max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.1). Walk me through fitting AND honestly evaluating on the test set.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: asks for/uses the absolute path, calls scripts/load_data.py, reads titanic_description.md. Adds the training/test split with stratification: df = df.with_columns(training=rsm.model.make_train(df, strat_var='survived', test_size=0.3, random_state=1234)). Explicitly justifies using the conservative max_depth=3 and learning_rate=0.1 over the pyrsm defaults (max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.3) which are too aggressive for small datasets like Titanic. Fits with rsm.model.xgboost(data={'titanic (train)': df.filter(pl.col('training') == 1)}, rvar='survived', lev='Yes', evar=['pclass', 'sex', 'age'], n_estimators=100, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.1, random_state=1234, mod_type='classification'). Prints summary() and notes the IN-SAMPLE AUC reported (around 0.89 with conservative max_depth=3 / lr=0.1) is on the TRAINING DATA and is OVEROPTIMISTIC — explicitly flags this as the central XGBoost trap: unlike Random Forest, XGBoost has NO OOB, so the summary's AUC reflects memorization. Then computes the HONEST test AUC: attaches predictions to all rows with df = df.with_columns(pred_xgb=xgb.predict(df).get_column('prediction')), then computes rsm.model.perf.auc(rvar=test_df['survived'], pred=test_df['pred_xgb'], lev='Yes') ON THE TEST ROWS ONLY (typically around 0.86-0.87 with conservative hyperparameters). Reports BOTH numbers and explains the gap (in-sample ~0.89 vs test ~0.87 = ~0.02 gap with conservative settings, which is healthy — much wider gaps appear with default max_depth=6 and lr=0.3). Recommends reporting the test AUC in any writeup. Optionally runs the gains/lift on train vs test to show the gap visually, and runs xgb.plot('pip') for permutation importance.

evals.prompt: Same titanic data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet. The XGBoost baseline got test AUC ~0.84. Can I do better by tuning learning_rate, n_estimators, and max_depth together? Run a grid search and refit.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) Sets up the train/test split as in eval 1. (2) Fits a baseline xgboost. (3) Constructs a small grid that tunes the three knobs JOINTLY: param_grid = {'max_depth': [2, 3, 4], 'learning_rate': [0.05, 0.1, 0.2], 'n_estimators': [100, 200, 300]}. (4) EXPLAINS the learning_rate × n_estimators tradeoff explicitly: lower learning rate requires more rounds but generalizes better; tuning one without the other is a common mistake. (5) Calls cv = rsm.model.cross_validation(xgb_baseline, 'xgb-cv', param_grid, {'AUC': 'roc_auc'}) and notes the 27 × 5 = 135 fits are cached to disk. (6) Inspects cv.best_params_ and cv.best_score_. (7) Refits with the tuned params: xgb_tuned = rsm.model.xgboost(data={...}, rvar='survived', lev='Yes', evar=[...], random_state=1234, **cv.best_params_). (8) Evaluates on the test set: rsm.model.perf.auc(...) on test rows. (9) Compares train and test gains charts via rsm.model.perf.gains_plot(dct=...) — interprets the train-test gap: a small gap (< 0.02 AUC difference) means the model generalizes well; a large gap (> 0.05) means residual overfit. (10) Provides DIAGNOSTIC-DRIVEN tuning advice: if train-test gap is still large after tuning, reduce max_depth further, increase min_child_weight, or add subsample/colsample regularization. (11) Reinforces the broader lesson: 'always validate the tuned model on a held-out test set, NOT on the same data used for CV — CV gives you the best avg-validation-fold score, but the final held-out test is the honest report number'.

Conversation that: notices the path is not absolute (uses ~), asks the user for the absolute path before running anything else, does NOT silently expand the tilde or guess. (We use this case to verify the skill enforces the absolute-path requirement from Step 1 of SKILL.md.)

evals.prompt: I fit an XGBoost on /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet predicting survival, with default hyperparameters (n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.3). xgb.summary() reports AUC = 0.935. Pretty close to perfect. Can I report this in my model writeup as 'XGBoost achieves AUC of 0.935'?
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) IMMEDIATELY pushes back on reporting the summary's AUC as 'the model's AUC' — this is the explicit critical concept the skill is designed to surface; (2) Explains why: the AUC printed by xgb.summary() is computed on the TRAINING data — every row was seen by the model during fitting. With pyrsm's default hyperparameters (max_depth=6 is deep, learning_rate=0.3 is aggressive), the model can absorb a lot of training-data structure that doesn't generalize. The 0.935 in-sample AUC includes substantial MEMORIZATION on top of genuine signal. (3) Computes the HONEST test AUC: requires fitting on the training subset (df.filter(training == 1)), scoring the test rows (df.filter(training == 0)) via xgb.predict(test_df), then computing rsm.model.perf.auc on those test predictions. Reports the test AUC (typically ~0.87 for default hyperparameters on Titanic) and shows the gap: 0.935 in-sample vs ~0.87 test = ~0.065 memorization premium. (4) RECOMMENDS reporting the test AUC of ~0.87 in the writeup, NOT the in-sample 0.935. The in-sample number is a misleading representation of model quality. (5) Notes that XGBoost has NO OOB equivalent (unlike Random Forest), so the held-out test set is the ONLY way to get an honest estimate of out-of-sample performance. (6) Optionally suggests REDUCING the model capacity (max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.1) to shrink the train-test gap — a model with smaller gap is more reliable for deployment, even if its in-sample AUC is lower. (7) Reinforces: 'in-sample metrics are diagnostic, not reportable. For any classification model you fit, the headline number should be the test AUC (or a cross-validated estimate), not the summary's training AUC.' (8) Optionally also flags that high in-sample AUC + large train-test gap is a red flag for overfit — recommend running rsm.model.perf.gains_plot(dct={'train': ..., 'test': ...}) to visualize the gap directly.
